articles.title: Ireland 36-40 USA: Hosts blow 19-point lead in Tallaght in WXV Global Series clash
articles.summary: Ireland blew a 19-point lead to suffer a 40-36 loss to the USA in their opening game of the WXV Global Series.
articles.body:
A player-of-the-match performance from Freda Tafuna helped the United States secure victory against Ireland in the WXV Global Series; Ireland play Japan next weekend

Ireland blew a 19-point lead to suffer a 40-36 loss to the USA in their opening game of the WXV Global Series.

The hosts romped to a 17-0 lead in the first 20 minutes in Dublin, with Vicky Elmes Kinlan opening the scoring and Dannah O'Brien scoring a conversion.

Tries from Cliodhna Moloney-MacDonald and Aoife Wafer made it 24-12 at half-time.

Early in the second half Ireland extended their advantage to 19 points, leading 31-12.

But the visitors, led by a player-of-the-match performance from Freda Tafuna, patiently clawed their way back into the clash with four successive tries from Kathryn Treder, twice, Hallie Taufoou and Tafuna.

Tafuna's try, scored while Kinlan was in the sin-bin, set the tone for the USA's first win over Ireland since 2018.

Scott Bemand's side are back in action next weekend away to Japan on Sunday at the Dexcom Stadium.

articles.title: Rugby League Ashes 2025: Fortune favours the brave as England must seize their golden opportunity at Wembley, says Brian Carney
articles.summary: Sky Sports Rugby League's Brian Carney looks ahead to the Ashes; Three Test matches between England and rivals Australia will be held at Wembley Stadium, Everton's new Hill Dickinson Stadium, and Headingley; It marks the return of the Ashes for the first time since 2003
articles.body:
Australia arrive at Wembley without James Tedesco, Latrell Mitchell, Tom Trbojevic, Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow, Payne Haas, Zac Lomax or Xavier Coates - all among the best rugby players on the planet.

Through injuries, withdrawals, and shifting allegiances, the Kangaroos are without a number of star names.

By contrast, England - who historically enter the international season down on numbers due to a longer season - are missing only Matty Ashton and Victor Radley. It's a far cry from the 2017 World Cup final when they were missing key players such as Josh Hodgson and Sean O'Loughlin and paid the price in a tense 0-6 battle.

Tomorrow they will enter Wembley strong, in front of a record Test crowd. Of course there are headline Australian stars like Nathan Cleary but the supporting cast should not spook England.

England have made much of a club-like atmosphere in their camp and their time together over the last three years. Shaun Wane has stuck with the players he trusts. If that's the case, then combinations and fluidity should immediately be on show against a side that have had the bare minimum of minutes together. This Australia side is completely different than the one that won the Pacific Championships last year.

England were rightly tipped by many to beat Tonga and Samoa in the last two years. They were superb in justifying their favourites tag and dismantled them with ease at times.

Historically there has been an aura around the Green and Gold that meant that the game was often lost before the players even got on the pitch. I remember that from being part of the Lions team in the 00s. But this is not a settled Kangaroos camp. In the build-up there was talk of disorganised preparation, as Mal Meninga walked away to recruit players for an NRL side that only starts in 2027. In his place comes Kevin Walters, who coached in the Super League fifteen years ago, with little success.

The question everyone in the game is asking is whether this is the unbeatable green and gold machine of old. Or is it a side distracted by the cult of State of Origin, their sacred ground, while the international jersey has gathered dust? The last time these two nations played, England were an ankle tap away from tying a game that may have ended in glory. The tragedy is that because they haven't played each other for eight years, we have no idea how the game will go. But that in itself brings excitement and intrigue.

The brilliant work done by players and administrators down under to push international rugby league back to the top of the pile should be commended. But the only way to kick on now is to see England play their part and win their first series since 1970.

As a member of the 2003 Lions team that could have won 3-0, but ended up losing 3-0, I know that narrow defeats count for nothing. Having played in teams that have sporadically beaten Australia home and away over the years I know a 2-1 series defeat counts for nothing either.

They, like me, will find out that if they don't seize this moment, there is no glory in defeat. It will be an opportunity wasted, and one that the players may never get the chance to rectify.

The stage is theirs. The time is now. This is the best chance England have ever had. Now they have to go and make the most of it. Fortune favours the brave.

First Test: Saturday October 25, Wembley Stadium, London

Second Test: Saturday November 1, Everton Stadium, Liverpool

Third Test: Saturday November 8, Headingley Stadium, Leeds

articles.title: Super League receive investment offer from Australia's National Rugby League as part of 'recapitalisation project'
articles.summary: Super League have received an investment offer from Australia Rugby League Commission (ARLC) who run the NRL; Sky Sports will show every game of the Super League live this season - including two matches in each round exclusively live
articles.body:
Conversations have long been occurring between Australia's governing body and Europe's, with a formal offer now having been received.

In a statement, Super League said: "RL Commercial can confirm that a first offer has been received from the ARLC (Australian Rugby League Commission) as part of the sport's recapitalisation project.

"The Super League clubs have been informed this morning.

"Details of the offer remain confidential."

Former NRL chief executive Andrew Abdo spoke to Sky Sports back in April about the NRL's planned involvement in Super League. He was over in the UK for talks about the move.

He said it was a move focused on the "globalisation" of rugby league with a view to ensure that rugby league in the UK and Europe is governed by an independent commission, similar to the set up of the ARLC.

ARLC Chairman Peter V'Landys is now understood to be leading the talks.

"We really believe in the globalisation of rugby league," Abdo told Sky Sports .

"This is a great game and we want to take it to as many people as possible. We want to win as many fans as possible.

"So while the game is growing really well in the southern hemisphere, we also want the game to be strong here in the north.

"This is about a partnership where we can collaborate on how we can grow the game, how we can grow revenues and how can those revenues be pumped back into the game?

"That's pretty nuanced and that's something we have to develop together."

RL Commercial managing director Rhodri Jones added on the talks from April: "They would like to have a heavy influence on the commission and who sits on that commission.

"What they perhaps haven't understood in totality is the make up of our governance structure in this country.

"We have multiple organisations in RFL, Super League and RL Commercial. When it is such a big topic like recapitalisation, it is complex.

"But with hard work, better detail, we can overcome some of these challenges so we can get to the right result that the sport wants."

The talks have now moved into the next negotiation phase.

articles.title: South Africa vs New Zealand live on Sky Sports: The history of 'rugby's greatest rivalry' ahead of four-Test series
articles.summary: We chronicle rugby rivalry between All Blacks and Springboks from 1921-2026: South Africa's apartheid era, contentious World Cup finals, respective periods on top; watch New Zealand's tour of South Africa live on Sky Sports+, with first Test on Saturday August 22 (4.10pm)
articles.body:
It's been advertised in New Zealand and South Africa as "Rugby's Greatest Rivalry Tour." A series of games to celebrate over a century of contests between the two most successful nations the sport has seen.

The All Blacks have already played and beaten the Stormers, Sharks and Bulls so far, and face the Springboks in Tests on August 22, August 29, September 5 and September 12.

So, what is the history between the two? And what have been the flashpoints and major moments over the decades? We take a look...

New Zealand and South Africa first met on August 13, 1921 in Carisbrook, Dunedin as part of South Africa's three-Test tour, with the All Blacks coming out with a 13-5 victory.

South Africa won a week later at Eden Park 9-5, with the third Test a 0-0 draw in Wellington to see the series end 1-1. And so set in motion a rugby rivalry which has endured right at the apex of the sport.

That first match included, there have been some 110 Test meetings, the All Blacks winning 63, South Africa 43 and four draws.

There have been 54 Tests played in South Africa, with the hosts winning 28, New Zealand 25 and one draw, while 48 Tests in New Zealand have seen the All Blacks win 34, Springboks 11 and three draws.

At Rugby World Cups, South Africa have beaten New Zealand in two dramatic finals (1995, 2023), and in one third-place playoff (1999), while New Zealand have beaten South Africa in the 2015 semi-finals, 2003 quarter-finals and 2023 pool stages.

After that original 1921 tour, the next time the sides met came in 1927 when New Zealand toured South Africa and again, the series finished in a captivating draw: 2-2 this time with wins for the Boks in Durban and Port Elizabeth, and wins for the All Blacks in Johannesburg and Cape Town.

South Africa won the next two series between the sides, touring New Zealand in 1937 and winning 2-1, while hosting the All Blacks in 1949 and winning 4-0.

In 1956, New Zealand get their own back as they clinched a 3-1 home series success over the Springboks, though 1960 saw South Africa back to winning ways via a 2-1 series win back on home soil.

South Africa's apartheid era, worldwide sporting ban and protests

Between 1948 and 1994, though, South Africa enforced apartheid, the institutionalised racial segregation and white minority rule.

As part of this shameful system, South Africa refused to allow people of different races to play sport together, with officials requesting Māori players not be involved in series between the nations. New Zealand agreed and excluded some of their finest players from several tours, with the first major public protests coming during that 1960 tour to South Africa.

By 1964, South Africa as a sporting nation were barred from participating at the Tokyo Olympic Games, and in 1970 they were formally expelled from the International Olympic Committee. They were excluded from international tennis and the Davis Cup the same year.

Throughout the rest of the 1970s, widespread cancellations and bans for South Africa in international sport continued, but rugby proved one of the last to take action.

Indeed, 1965 saw South Africa tour New Zealand with the All Blacks winning three Tests to one, before the Halt All Racist Tours protest group was established in New Zealand in 1969 to oppose continued tours to and from South Africa.

The All Blacks toured South Africa in 1970 in any case, losing 3-1 to the Springboks, and though a 1973 tour to New Zealand was cancelled amid a climate of South Africa's worldwide sporting expulsion, series between the nations still took place in 1976 and 1981 - South Africa winning the former at home 3-1, and New Zealand the latter series 2-1 which was dogged by protests and worldwide condemnation.

Indeed, during that 1981 tour two games were cancelled. One in Hamilton saw 200 protestors rip down a chain fence, sprinkle nails all over the pitch and stage a sit-in on the halfway line, while a match against South Canterbury at Timaru was cancelled because the authorities said they would not be able to control demonstrations there.

During the final Test of the tour, an aircraft continually flew overhead the pitch and dropped flour bombs, flares and leaflets in protest. All Blacks prop Gary Knight was temporarily stunned by a flour bomb.

Eventually, the planned 1985 series between the two was cancelled in line with South Africa's wider sporting ban, with a legal ruling in New Zealand determining it would be "incompatible with the NZRFU's legally stated purpose of fostering and encouragement of the game of rugby."

The Springboks were barred from rugby's first two World Cups in 1987 and 1991, while a 1986 British and Irish Lions tour was also cancelled.

After the 1985 series between South Africa and New Zealand was cancelled, a 'rebel tour' which was not government-sanctioned was organised, and a team travelled in 1986 called New Zealand Cavaliers. The Kiwi players involved received condemnation, were banned for several Tests after the tour and some never played for New Zealand again.

South Africa's return to international sport and contentious World Cup glory

Upon the end of the apartheid regime, South Africa organised a Test against the All Blacks in 1992 for their first encounter since being welcomed back to international sport, and even went on to surprisingly win it 27-24 at Ellis Park.

With the released Nelson Mandela inaugurated as president in 1994, he encouraged all South Africans to back the previously hated Springboks.

In 1994, South Africa toured New Zealand for the first time in nearly 20 years, losing two Tests and drawing one, with South Africa then hosting the 1995 Rugby World Cup.

Ranked ninth in the world after their lengthy period of sporting exile, South Africa shocked many by progressing to the final where Jonah Lomu and the All Blacks awaited.

A fairytale 15-12 World Cup final victory over New Zealand at Ellis Park followed, but was there foul play involved?

The All Blacks had outscored their opponents 315-104 en route to the final, and were heavy, heavy favourites, yet they failed to score a single try in a contest that went through extra- time. How?

For many, the reason lies with the fact that a hefty proportion of the New Zealand team were struck down by illness or food poisoning on the cusp of the final.

For All Blacks head coach at the time, Laurie Mains, the culprit was a disappearing waitress named 'Suzie' - a conspiracy theory that was never proven, though Mains even hired a private investigator after the final. Team doctor Mike Bowen has also always insisted the All Blacks were poisoned, as has South African security guard Rory Steyn.

What is indisputable is that a large majority of the All Blacks squad were struck down with violent illness in the days before a World Cup final against the Springboks in South Africa.

New Zealand's 'Incomparables' and period of dominance

A little over a year after that World Cup final, the All Blacks toured South Africa in August 1996 set on revenge.

They had already beaten the Springboks home and away during the inaugural 1996 Tri-Nations, clinching the title, but a three-Test tour in South Africa against the world champions was built up as the next major challenge.

In New Zealand, that side are now known as 'The Incomparables,' as they played some magnificent rugby to launch rugby's era of professionalism, winning the first Test 23-19 in Durban, and then the second Test 33-26 at Loftus Versfeld in Pretoria, clinching the series with a Test to spare.

South Africa won that third Test, but it mattered little as the All Blacks kicked on to win 13 of the next 17 contests - going unbeaten against the Boks between 2001 and July 2004. Tri-Nations titles followed in 1997, 1999, 2002 and 2003.

The Springboks landed Tri-Nations titles in 2004 and 2009, but outside of those years, New Zealand firmly established themselves as the premier nation on the globe.

The All Blacks won Tri-Nations titles four years in a row between 2005 and 2008, again in 2010, then three more years in a row between 2011 and 2013, and three more years in a row again between 2016 and 2018. They also lifted Rugby World Cup titles in 2011 and 2015 - the latter with a side many consider the greatest ever.

They were caught by France at the 2007 World Cup despite being huge favourites, as South Africa went on to lift their second Webb Ellis Trophy, but the Boks failed to clinch silverware in any form between 2009 and 2019.

September 16, 2017 proved one of South Africa's darkest rugby days, when they travelled to Albany and were defeated 57-0 by the All Blacks.

They were beaten by Ireland 38-3 in Dublin two months later, losing to Wales in Cardiff the same Test window. Such form followed a 2016 in which the Springboks were soundly beaten by England and Wales, lost to Italy for the first time, were beaten by Argentina and Australia, lost to Ireland at home and went down 57-15 to the All Blacks.

Enough was enough, and so heralded the era of Rassie Erasmus.

The controversial, unusual rugby head coach of the Springboks totally turned around South Africa's fortunes.

By September 2018, a rejuvenated, confident side travelled to New Zealand and picked up a shock 36-34 victory in Wellington - a first win on Kiwi soil since 2009.

A little over a year later, South Africa became world champions for the third time, clinching World Cup glory vs England in the final in Japan - Eddie Jones' side having dealt with the All Blacks in the semi-finals, after the latter had beaten South Africa during the pool stages.

Since that tournament, in 11 Tests between South Africa and New Zealand, the Springboks have won seven of them, winning Rugby Championship crowns in 2024 and 2025, and the 2023 Rugby World Cup final - albeit the latter victory came in fortunate fashion, it must be said, against a 14-player All Blacks side who probably deserved victory.

If the 2023 South Africa side was strong, the current one is likely even better, with greater depth, while the All Blacks are looking to rebuild again under Dave Rennie, with Scott Robertson having been sacked.

"With eight matches in six weeks, including a four-Test series against the Springboks, this would have to be the toughest tour in rugby," Rennie said.

"It will be an intense seven weeks of touring but an excellent opportunity for us to pit ourselves against the current benchmark team in world rugby, and to build connections with each other in a way that only a tour of this scale can do."

articles.title: South Africa vs New Zealand: Can All Blacks weather Springboks backlash to cement progress in Cape Town
articles.summary: New Zealand stand on the brink of history as South Africa face a must-win Test in Cape Town; can the Springboks strike back or will the All Blacks prove their rise is no flash in the pan; watch South Africa vs New Zealand live from 4.55pm on Sky Sports Action
articles.body:
The All Blacks had better brace themselves. South Africa do not take too kindly to losing at home, let alone in the manner in which their challenge unravelled in last week's 33-16 loss at Ellis Park.

The Springboks will undoubtedly come back harder in Cape Town, with a response essential if they are to keep their hopes of winning this four-Test series alive. A draw can still be salvaged if they lose again, but for an all-conquering South Africa side with a taste for success, nothing but victory will surely do.

The reigning back-to-back world champions and Rugby Championship holders have lost just one home Test series in the last 30 years. With another defeat moving them a step closer to an unwanted piece of history, a swift response is required.

A phenomenon seen across sport is the paradigm of the chaser versus the chased. For seven years, South Africa have been the dominant force in world rugby, as their successive World Cup titles attest. They have been the benchmark, the standard that other nations have sought to emulate.

That daunting task is perhaps only dwarfed by the one South Africa have successfully wrestled with: staying ahead of the curve and constantly evolving while remaining one step ahead of their rivals.

It is a challenge New Zealand now face as Dave Rennie is tasked with cementing the All Blacks' position as the world's No 1-ranked side.

With the pressure on South Africa to respond, New Zealand can play with a freedom not afforded to the Springboks. But being the hunter is one thing. Remaining the hunted is another.

Can the All Blacks cement their progress?

Standalone victories against South Africa in South Africa may not have been as rare as, say, victories over New Zealand at Eden Park, but successive Test victories over the Springboks certainly are.

They have been non-existent in the Rassie Erasmus era. In fact, you have to go back to the 2015 Rugby Championship, when South Africa lost to New Zealand and Argentina, for the last time the Springboks suffered successive home Test defeats.

The All Blacks have not won a Test series in South Africa since 1996 but stand one victory away from ensuring a drawn series at the very least.

New Zealand absorbed immense pressure, scrum dominance and territorial control from the Springboks at Ellis Park before ruthlessly punishing South African errors.

If there was a surprise element to the tactics New Zealand deployed in Johannesburg, make no mistake those will be addressed by the Springboks this week.

With the All Blacks set to face a very different, wounded animal this time around, the question is whether their game has enough facets to withstand the inevitable backlash and prove their rise is about more than one impressive performance in Johannesburg.

Should it happen, a first series defeat to the All Blacks on home soil since 1996 would be a tough pill to swallow for the reigning back-to-back world champions, but history suggests it may ultimately prove a blessing in disguise.

Under Erasmus' stewardship, South Africa's dominance has been built on learning from defeat and implementing change.

Pool-stage losses to New Zealand and Ireland at the 2019 and 2023 World Cups served as fuel to propel the Boks to back-to-back titles.

With little more than a year to go until they defend their crown in Australia, should this thorough New Zealand examination continue, further lessons may emerge that can be channelled into the pursuit of yet more silverware.

articles.title: South Africa 33-26 New Zealand: Cheslin Kolbe stars with the boot as Springboks level series in Cape Town
articles.summary: Springboks strike back in Cape Town to level Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series with All Blacks; four-Test battle moves to Johannesburg for third clash on September 5; watch every minute of New Zealand's tour of South Africa exclusively live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
The sides shared seven tries, with Jesse Kriel, Damian de Allende and Kolisi crossing for the Springboks, either side of scores from Cam Roigard, Damian McKenzie and Leroy Carter. But Cheslin Kolbe's 18 points from the tee ultimately proved decisive.

All Blacks captain Ardie Savea added a late fourth try for New Zealand - his 33rd in Test rugby - as the visitors finished with four tries to South Africa's three, but they were unable to overcome Kolbe's flawless accuracy.

Savea had predicted before kick-off that New Zealand would face a "wounded beast", and South Africa delivered an immediate response. Kriel crossed inside the opening two minutes, only for Roigard to hit back midway through a breathless opening quarter.

Kolbe's first penalty and de Allende's try either side of the 20-minute mark reasserted South African control. McKenzie's converted score kept the All Blacks within touching distance, but Kolisi crashed over on the stroke of half-time to send the hosts into the break with a 24-14 lead.

The 32-year-old's boot then tightened South Africa's grip after the break, with two penalties in three minutes stretching the lead beyond two scores. Carter's unconverted try briefly gave the All Blacks hope, but the wing's fourth penalty effectively settled the contest.

"We know last week we let it slip," said Kolbe, who was named player of the match. "We could feel the mood from the South Africa fans. We just wanted to do the jersey proud, our families proud.

"You need to take every point given to you. That's Test match rugby. We stuck to the plan to take the points on offer."

Savea admitted the All Blacks had paid for their slow start.

"We kind of let the Springboks get ahead in the first two minutes and we were chasing the game," said the New Zealand captain. "We stuck in there but we came up short. It's a tough pill to swallow.

"We lost the battle tonight but we haven't lost the war. We'll get back on the horse this week and go again."

The New Zealand captain also paid tribute to Pieter-Steph du Toit, who won his 100th cap, and Ox Nche, who won his 50th, for their respective milestones.

"It's been a massive week," Kolisi said. "Last week we didn't take our opportunities but this week we did. Coach Rassie [Erasmus] always reminds us that this is not just about us, it's about all of South Africa. We knew that the mood was down this past week.

"Next week is going to be big. Some of us are playing for the first time in Soweto. It's hard playing them once. Playing them four times in a row is incredibly difficult."

Defeat would have handed South Africa successive home losses for the first time since 2015, but Erasmus' side instead travel to Johannesburg with momentum restored.

South Africa shut out pre-match disruption to level series

South Africa's preparations were anything but settled in the build-up to the game.

Erasmus made five changes to the team he had originally named, with Handre Pollard and Kurt-Lee Arendse withdrawing on Friday. That prompted the head coach to recall Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu at fly-half, just a week after dropping him, while Kolbe was brought into the starting XV on the wing.

There was another late twist an hour before kick-off when Deon Fourie, Gerhard Steenekamp and Thomas du Toit were promoted to the starting front row. Malcolm Marx, Ox Nche and Wilco Louw consequently dropped to the bench, with no reason given for the last-minute reshuffle.

On a more positive note, Kolisi returned to captain the side after missing the opening Test, while two-time World Rugby Player of the Year Du Toit celebrated his 100th Test cap.

New Zealand made three changes from their victory at Ellis Park, with winger Leroy Carter replacing Josh Moorby, while George Bower and Tupou Vaa'i came into the pack for Ethan de Groot and Josh Lord, who were both ruled out with concussion. Ruben Love retained the fly-half jersey, while Beauden Barrett was again left out of the matchday 23.

The All Blacks' five-try, 33-16 victory in Johannesburg had lifted them above the world champions to the top of the world rankings, giving Dave Rennie's side the early advantage in the first full Test series between the nations in three decades.

But the response South Africa demanded duly arrived in Cape Town. The Springboks levelled the series at 1-1 and extended a formidable home record that has seen them lose just one series on South African soil in the past 30 years.

The tour, billed as Rugby's Greatest Rivalry, is New Zealand's first full visit to South Africa since 1996. The All Blacks arrived in Cape Town unbeaten on the trip, having defeated the Stormers, Sharks and Bulls before narrowly escaping with victory over the Lions in a midweek clash in Johannesburg.

The series now moves to FNB Stadium for the third Test on September 5, before concluding with a historic first meeting on American soil at Baltimore's M&T Bank Stadium on September 12.

articles.summary: South Africa beat New Zealand in thrilling third Test to secure 2-1 series lead and hand Siya Kolisi his record 55th victory as Springboks captain; series concludes with fourth and final Test in Baltimore, USA, on Saturday, live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
The Springboks and All Blacks traded four tries apiece in a pulsating contest that was as brutal as it was captivating in front of a capacity crowd of 87,976 in Soweto.

Kurt-Lee Arendse, Jesse Kriel and Malcolm Marx crossed for the Springboks, who were also awarded a penalty try, as they followed last week's narrow victory in Cape Town with another hard-fought triumph.

New Zealand captain Ardie Savea scored two first-half tries before suffering a game-ending shoulder injury, while record try-scorer Will Jordan and hooker Samisoni Taukei'aho crossed late on for the All Blacks.

The teams now travel to Baltimore, USA, for the final instalment of the four-Test series, live on Sky Sports, where nothing less than victory will do for the All Blacks if they are to salvage something.

Springboks seize control of New Zealand series

It was another classic clash of Springbok forward power against flowing All Blacks attack, with New Zealand flying out of the blocks before being overwhelmed by South Africa's second-half surge.

The visitors struck first through captain Savea, who finished a quick line-out move after Asafo Aumua had charged at the home defence.

Arendse responded for the Springboks, diving over in the corner after a strong Damian de Allende handed Leroy Carter off.

Savea grabbed his second five minutes later, gathering a loose ball to score after Carter had burst down the left wing, but his afternoon ended early with a shoulder injury before South Africa's scrum forced a penalty try to level on the stroke of half-time.

Jordan restored New Zealand's lead and ignited the second half with his 54th Test try only for Kriel to race through after Carter missed another tackle.

That spark proved decisive, with Springboks might showcased by Marx's maul try and then underscored by Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu's penalty as Samisoni Taukei'aho's late score proved nothing more than a consolation.

"We're so proud of the win today. It was a great game from the All Blacks. They pushed us to the limit, they came like a house on fire.

"That first 25 minutes, our lungs were pumping hard. We did so well to make sure we didn't concede more points and fight back. The way we finished at the end was a lot better than we did the last two weeks.

"We play for ourselves, for the Springboks, but most importantly, we play for the people of South Africa. We represent each and every single person here.

"We're thankful and grateful that we have the privilege, not pressure, to be able to change people's moods and make them feel good."

articles.title: Argentina 28-28 Australia: Wallabies claim series win after draw in ill-disciplined final Test in Mendoza
articles.summary: Argentina were reduced to 13 players for the closing stages, which proved decisive as Australia claimed a series win; Watch the fourth and final Test between South Africa and New Zealand in Baltimore, USA, live on Sky Sports Action on Saturday from 10pm
articles.body:
The Wallabies, who won 27-21 when the two sides met last week, scored tries through Harry Wilson and Max Jorgensen in the first half before Fraser McReight went over in the second and a penalty try with 10 minutes to go secured the draw.

Pablo Matera scored a brace for Argentina, along with scores from Ignacio Mendy and Ignacio Ruiz, but they will be left to rue ill discipline from Lucio Cinti and Santiago Carreras in the closing stages which denied them the chance to chase victory.

Australia had a try ruled out on 16 minutes when McReight went out of touch, but they did score four minutes later when Wilson beat two tacklers and touched down with Ryan Lonergan adding the extras.

Shortly afterwards, Franco Molina was yellow carded for Argentina and Australia extended their lead when Jorgensen found the line - but the home side responded with two tries in three minutes after Australia lock Jeremy Williams was sin-binned.

Firstly, Matera finished off a fine passage of play from close range and then Mendy scored following tremendous work from Joaquin Moro and Carreras slotted the conversion to level the scores at 14-14.

McReight restored Australia's lead seven minutes after half-time when he forced his way through three Argentina players only to see Ruiz dot down from close range eight minutes later as Argentina levelled up once more.

The home side finally took the lead when Matera scored his second try with 16 minutes to go, touching down between the posts after 23 phases of play.

But just five minutes later, Cinti was given a yellow card for a deliberate knock-on and Australia took advantage with a penalty try moments later.

A pass intended for Filipo Daugunu which would have resulted in a certain score was deliberately blocked by the outstretched hand of Carreras. He was sent to the sin bin, reducing Argentina to 13 men with 10 minutes to go.

Australia pushed for the victory in the closing stages, but couldn't get across the line and settled for a victory in the series if not on the night.

Wallabies take impressive summer form into South Africa Test

The Wallabies leave Argentina with their unbeaten record intact over the two-Test series, but captain Wilson - while complimentary of his side's achievements - was disappointed not to maintain their winning run ahead of a daunting next Test at home to world champions South Africa on September 27.

" In that last 10 minutes, they played the conditions really well, knowing they're a few men down. It's a bit slippery on the deck and they just tried to hold on to the ball for as long as they can," Wilson said.

"We've obviously had a few wins in a row and to get a draw tonight is not ideal.

"But to bring another trophy home, it hopefully brings a bit of momentum and some confidence in the group going to the Springboks."

Despite remaining realistic about his side's shortcomings, head coach Les Kiss shared his skipper's positivity after what has been an impressive summer for a reinvigorated Australia side who haven't lost any of their four Tests in 2026.

"Securing that trophy is definitely one of the things that we came here to do, without a doubt," Kiss said.

"Talking to the lads, very pleased that that part of the equation was on point.

"We probably took control of patches of that game and put ourselves in a good position to win it but as it is over here, it's tough. The boys are a little bit disappointed that they just didn't go on with it for sure.

"Mixed feelings in a way but there is something that we did come here to achieve and we got that. The rugby bit is trying to get some areas of our game a little bit better and a bit more robust and we've got things to work on for sure."

articles.title: England rugby squad: Captain Maro Itoje returns but Courtney Lawes and Joe Marchant made to wait after Prem returns
articles.summary: Lawes and Marchant are available for selection after returning from French clubs, but Steve Borthwick wants to see how they bed back into the Gallagher Prem before deciding on their international futures; Archie McParland and Kepueli Tuipulotu get call-ups
articles.body:
Itoje was rested for the Nations Championship games against South Africa, Fiji and Argentina but features in a 36-man group that will begin preparations for the autumn with a three-day camp starting on Sunday.

The Saracens second row is expected to resume as captain for the opener against Australia at Allianz Stadium on November 8, taking over from Jamie George who deputised in July.

Lawes and Marchant have become available for selection since returning from French clubs Brive and Stade Francais, respectively, after their moves across the Channel put their England careers on hold.

However, it is understood head coach Steve Borthwick wants to see how they bed back into the Gallagher Prem before deciding whether to include them in future squads.

Both players were part of the 2023 World Cup squad, with Lawes' progress of particular interest given the experience and leadership he would bring to an England set-up that needs those assets.

Highly-rated prop Fin Baxter is back after a series of foot problems kept him out since December while exciting rookies Archie McParland and Kepueli Tuipulotu are included.

Scrum-half McParland looked set to tour during the summer only for a nasty leg wound sustained in Northampton's victory over Exeter in the Prem final to rule him out.

Alex Mitchell (hamstring) and Ben Spencer (shoulder) are more established options at half-back but both are rehabbing with their clubs, giving McParland the chance to impress Borthwick.

Max Ojomoh (calf) and Noah Clauori (wrist) are unavailable, while Tom Roebuck's selection for Sale on Sunday prevents him from being involved.

George and Ollie Chessum have joined up with England but are receiving treatment for respective groin and foot problems.

articles.body:
Led by captain Megan Jones, the squad contains a combined 1,234 international caps, while there are three as yet uncapped players picked in the form of Bryony Field, Hayley Jones and Sophie McQueen.

England take on Australia at CorpAcq Stadium in the outskirts of Manchester on Saturday September 12, before meeting Canada in a repeat of their 2025 World Cup final clash at Sandy Park, Exeter, a week later.

Rounding off the home leg of the series is a mouth-watering matchup against New Zealand at Allianz Stadium in front of over 50,000 spectators on Saturday September 26.

Mitchell said: "It's been a positive pre-season in the way we have trained and the exposure we have given to players. The girls have worked hard to elevate their connections, making us stronger, and have driven high standards.

"We have trained above the game level with great intensity and now we have an opportunity to excite ourselves, and the country, by the way we play rugby in three Test matches across the country.

"This squad is only four weeks old; there is plenty in the tank. This is an exciting period to get after."

The 2026 season is the inaugural edition of the WXV Global Series. The 12 participating nations are fixed for the 2026-2028 cycle, with no promotion or relegation.

articles.title: South Africa vs New Zealand: Rassie Erasmus urges Springboks to risk more as All Blacks series finale looms in Baltimore
articles.summary: South Africa are 2-1 up in four-Test series vs New Zealand; All Blacks took first Test with superb victory at Ellis Park, but Springboks then won second and third; series concludes with fourth and final Test in Baltimore, USA, on Saturday live on Sky Sports NFL from 10pm
articles.body:
The Springboks, from 1-0 down, seek to win the series 3-1 on Saturday at the home of the NFL's Baltimore Ravens, while the All Blacks are hoping to square the first traditional series between them in 30 years.

South Africa scored one try in the first Test which they lost, three tries in the second Test which they won, and four in last weekend's third Test where they were at their most expansive yet.

Their traditional set-piece strength was decisive - a penalty try from a pushover scrum and a lineout maul that marched New Zealand back to its posts - but the forwards' fearsome power was complemented by two well-taken backline tries.

"Damian [de Allende] was good on Saturday, Jesse [Kriel] was very good, Ethan [Hooker] did well, so the guys are getting better," Erasmus said on Monday at the team announcement.

Erasmus believed they might have put too much focus in the first Test on stopping New Zealand and not taking more risks in a game they controlled for the first hour at Ellis Park.

"At the end of the day you just need to outscore your opposition," Erasmus said. "If it means they score four tries and you kick five drop-goals like Jannie de Beer at the 1999 World Cup against England, you just need to score more points than them.

"To try and contain them is extremely difficult - just ask our franchises and France."

Only two SA changes made...for now! | Mo'unga returns for All Blacks

Erasmus has made two changes to the side which beat New Zealand 29-24 last Saturday for this weekend's fourth Test.

Damian Willemse returns to full-back for the injured Cheslin Kolbe, and scrum-half Morné van den Berg was given his first start in the series, dropping Cobus Reinach to the bench.

Yet, that may not be the end of things as since first Test defeat, Erasmus has played fast and loose in terms of making late changes to his team selections.

Before the second Test, named in the front row for the Springboks were Ox Nche, Malcolm Marx and Wilco Louw. Just one hour before kick-off, that was changed to Gerhard Steenekamp, Deon Fourie and Thomas du Toit with the original three dropping to the bench.

"We feel that the team is well settled and all the players delivered in their respective roles in the last two matches, so we believe selecting the same matchday squad, and naming Damian back in his regular position makes sense," Erasmus said.

Kolbe broke his jaw making a tackle. He covered for Willemse, who suffered a hamstring problem in the second Test.

"It's good to have [Willemse] back," Erasmus said. "He knows the guys around him very well, so it will simply be a matter of him picking up where he left off before last week."

As for the No 9 jersey, Erasmus rewarded Van den Berg for "a fantastic impact" off the bench.

For New Zealand, the headline team news is the return of Richie Mo'unga at fly-half in what will be his first Test appearance since the 2023 Rugby World Cup final, having moved to play club rugby in Japan in the intervening years. Ruben Love drops out of the matchday 23 altogether.

Further changes were guaranteed after series-ending injuries to captain and No 8 Ardie Savea (shoulder), flanker Luke Jacobson (elbow) and centre Quinn Tupaea (knee). Lock Fabian Holland is also unavailable due to illness.

Hooker Codie Taylor comes in from the cold to captain the side, while prop Fletcher Newell, lock Patrick Tuipulotu, back-row Ethan Blackadder and centre Anton Lienert-Brown come in for their first starts of the series. Beauden Barrett and Rieko Ioane return to the bench.

"We always planned for there to be a number of changes for this match. Every player here has worked incredibly hard over the last seven weeks to prepare the team for the seven games we've played so far, and all those selected for this Test fully deserve it," head coach Dave Rennie said.

"We have everything to play for on Saturday. It is our chance to draw the series and end the tour with a performance to be proud of."

articles.title: Steve Borthwick: England head coach set for contract extension beyond 2028 Six Nations
articles.summary: Steve Borthwick is set to have his England contract extended beyond the 2028 Six Nations; the RFU will hand Borthwick the extension to avoid uncertainty around his future before and during next year's World Cup
articles.body:
The RFU will hand Borthwick the extension to avoid uncertainty around his future before and during next year's World Cup.

RFU performance director Conor O'Shea said: "You don't want them looking for a job going into [a World Cup].

"Everyone knows it will be judged on the World Cup, but you can't have a group of coaches going in with that uncertainty, especially when you look at the timing.

"So we will give that certainty, and that will give us time to look properly."

Borthwick has been back to lead England to the World Cup, following a "challenging" Six Nations review.

England came into the 2026 championship on an 11-Test winning run, but despite starting with victory over Wales they ended up suffering four defeats from five including away to Italy for the first time in history and a record home loss to Ireland.

The end result was Borthwick's side finishing fifth in the Six Nations standings just over 18 months before the next Rugby World Cup in Australia in 2027.

Last week, RFU CEO Bill Sweeney said Borthwick would be backed after a review into England's worst-ever Six Nations showing.

"This has been a thorough and honest review, and it is clear that improvement will come from addressing several areas rather than chasing one simple answer," Sweeney said.

"Steve has engaged in this process with full openness and has clear plans in place to address these findings. We are all behind him and his coaching team going into the Nations Championship and the series of matches leading into Rugby World Cup 2027."

Meanwhile, Courtney Lawes and Joe Marchant must outshine their domestic rivals when the Gallagher Premiership season starts after being warned they will not walk straight back into England's autumn squad.

Defence coach Richard Wigglesworth has outlined what is required from the Sale duo in the five competitive fixtures that take place before Borthwick names his squad for the second phase of the Nations Championship.

Lawes and Marchant, members of the 2023 World Cup squad, have become available for England selection again after returning from spells at French clubs to join the Sharks over the summer.

Both players would be valuable assets for Borthwick, Test centurion Lawes providing experience, leadership and back-row pedigree while Marchant offers another option in the problematic midfield department.

England will closely monitor their progress over the coming weeks and for all their pedigree, they need to prove themselves again.

"We want as much quality as we can have in the league but they are going to have to go and play well," Wigglesworth said.

"There are some good players in the room and to pick them you have to leave someone else out, so they would have to go over and above that I would say.

"It's great to have Courtney back. He has unbelievable experience, is an England legend and has been flying in pre-season, as everyone is.

"There is a real excitement about watching him back in the Prem, so I'm enjoying that.

"I have actually bumped into Joe Marchant walking around living quite close to me, so I caught up with him and it is great to have him back."

Lawes announced his retirement after the last World Cup but his return to these shores has reignited his desire to add to his 105 caps, raising the possibility of his involvement in Australia 2027 as a 38-year-old.

Under Rugby Football Union rules, only players competing in the Prem can be selected by Borthwick and by returning from France he comes into consideration.

"Everyone's case is individual in where you want to play your rugby and what you want to do," Wigglesworth said. "I couldn't have given up the chance of England because I didn't play as much as loads of people.

"But Courtney has said 'I've got an itch here and I'm coming back'. How good is that as a statement? 'I am coming back because I want to do this'.

"That level of determination and the qualities he has should put himself in a good spot. Experience, he has certainly got that. We are keen to watch him play."

articles.title: Red Roses vs Australia: England name team for opening WXV Global Series home match with Tatyana Heard, Natasha Hunt back from injury
articles.summary: Five changes to John Mitchell's side in first match since the end of the Women's Six Nations in May; England begin new WXV Global Series with three home matches this month against Australia, Canada and New Zealand
articles.body:
Head coach John Mitchell has made five changes from England's last match against France in May, when they secured their fifth successive Women's Six Nations Grand Slam.

World Cup winners Tatyana Heard (centre) and Natasha Hunt (scrum-half) return from injury to reclaim places in the XV.

Fly-half Holly Aitchison comes in to win her 50th international cap, May Campbell is selected at hooker and Wing Mia Venner forms the back three with Claudia Moloney-MacDonald and Ellie Kildunne.

Hannah Botterman, who missed the entire Six Nations, and Morwenna Talling are also available again and are named among the replacements.

Saracens prop Kelsey Clifford has been ruled out of the Red Roses' home WXV Global Series matches because of a hamstring injury, with Liz Crake replacing her in the squad. Clifford will remain as part of the training squad with a view of returning to play on the tour to North America in October.

Saturday's match against Australia takes place at CorpAcq Stadium, the home of the Gallagher Prem's Sale Sharks.

Mitchell, who had two stints at Sale, said: "I have very fond memories of the north west from my time with Sale Sharks so it's awesome to be able to take our game to this part of the country.

"Playing in a different part of the country allows us to be present in the community and keeps the game healthy. You've not only got to be visible, but if you can actually be close to your community, I think that's even better.

"Connection is such an important part of life, but particularly in sport. The girls have worked hard in pre-season to deepen their bond and that will make us stronger on the field.

"We're excited to get our WXV Global Series under way and aim to excite and entertain."

The 2026 season is the inaugural edition of the WXV Global Series. The 12 participating nations are fixed for the 2026-2028 cycle, with no promotion or relegation.

England next play Canada in a repeat of their 2025 World Cup final clash at Sandy Park, Exeter, on September 19 before facing New Zealand at Allianz Stadium on September 26.

The Red Roses tour Canada and the United States as part of the WXV series in October.

articles.title: South Africa vs New Zealand: Springboks show steel to secure 43-28 victory and 3-1 series win against All Blacks
articles.summary: South Africa entered the fourth Test with a 2-1 lead over New Zealand in the Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series; They increased that to 3-1 with a 43-28 victory at the home of NFL's Baltimore Ravens
articles.body:
South Africa had a narrow 17-14 half-time lead thanks to a Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu penalty plus converted tries from Damien De Allende and Morné van den Berg.

However, New Zealand had scored early through Cody Taylor and then hit again late on through Will Jordan, Damian McKenzie converting both to put his side just three points adrift with 40 minutes to play.

The game looked in the balance in the second half after converted tries from Malcolm Marx and Steph du Toit were met by an Ethan Blackadder effort.

However, Kurt-Lee Arendse took his opportunity to race away and score and was quickly followed up by Cameron Hanekom to seal a Springboks win, a Beauden Barrett late try merely a consolation.

Indeed, the Springboks took the win in front of the largest attendance ever at a rugby union match in the United States.

New Zealand went 1-0 up after a 33-16 win at Johannesburg's Ellis Park but then the Springboks hit back in the next two Tests. They won 33-26 in Cape Town and followed that up with a close 29-24 win at Soweto's FNB Stadium.

That meant Rugby's Greatest Rivalry had a grand finale in Baltimore which saw the Springboks prevail in the first traditional series between the two sides in 30 years.

Not only that, it was a victory that marked head coach Rassie Erasmus' 100th Test in charge.

USA sets stage for a Test to remember between two powerhouses

After a spine-tingling Haka from the All Blacks, the Baltimore crowd erupted as this fourth and final Test of the Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series got under way.

There was some early ill-discipline from both sides but as the game settled, and after an early Feinberg-Mngomezulu penalty, it was the All Blacks that crossed the whitewash first.

Some sensationally slick hands out to left edge opened the space for Taylor to run a fantastic line and score, McKenzie converting for a 7-3 lead.

The possession then all went in favour of the Springboks for much of the rest of the half. Poor handling from New Zealand gave away opportunities and off the back of a scrum, South Africa continuously powered over the gain line until De Allende eventually barrelled over and with the conversion, they had a 10-7 advantage after a breathless first 15 minutes.

After a brief break to fix a communication issue for the refereeing team, the game got back under way and South Africa pounced again on the 22nd minute. Off the back off the driving maul from five metres out Van den Berg through a delicious dummy to score.

Once again, the try was converted and it looked like South Africa had a comprehensive 17-7 lead. Frankly, they could have had more if they iced all their opportunities.

However, New Zealand were not done and just three minutes before half-time, and after 32 phases, the gap opened for Jordan to run through and score under the sticks for his 55th Test try.

The conversion from McKenzie had the game finely balanced at 17-14 with just 40 minutes of rugby remaining in this series.

South Africa made dominance pay in the second half when, off the back of a driving maul, Marx barrelled over and was quickly followed by Du Toit within the space of three minutes. Van den Berg converted the second try and with less than half an hour remaining, the Springboks had a 29-14 lead.

The All Blacks hit back through an Ethan Blackadder converted try which seemed to have the game finely poised at 29-21.

But, just as New Zealand looked to be firing in attack once again to race away and score, a knock on provided Arendse with an opportunity to show off his silky foot work, race away, and dive in under the sticks.

New Zealand's bubble was then firmly burst as, just four minutes later, Hanekom went over to make sure the series would go South Africa's way. Libbok converted both and a 43-21 lead looked enough.

Beauden Barrett did manage to add a late consolation try but it was merely that as South Africa showed once again why they are the No 1 team in world rugby.

South Africa captain Siya Kolisi speaking on Sky Sports...

"I want to thank every South African here in the stadium and back at home.

"It was a special week to see you come out in umbers and support us. We are so grateful.

"We could hear you today. Thank you so much.

"To the New Zealand supporters too, thank you for coming to our beautiful country and embracing our culture.

"We go hard on each other on the field but the respect we have for each other is always there."

articles.title: South Africa vs New Zealand: Record crowd in Baltimore provides 'appetiser' for 2031 Rugby World Cup on US soil
articles.summary: The fourth Test in the Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series between South Africa and New Zealand drew in a record crowd for rugby union on US soil; The teams are hoping it provides a strong start ahead of America hosting the Rugby World Cup in 2031
articles.body:
Saturday's crowd of 68,173 was the largest ever for a rugby international in the US. The colours speckling the stands revealed that most were in the green of South Africa, with a few black jerseys of New Zealand and a balance of interested neutrals.

They enjoyed an enthralling Test in which the Springboks ran out 43-28 winners to clinch a 3-1 series victory.

Rugby has tried for years to break into the lucrative American sporting market. Saturday's large and enthusiastic crowd suggested there might yet be a foothold.

Speaking after the clash, All Blacks captain Codie Taylor and his Springboks counterpart, Siya Kolisi, agreed that giving Americans more opportunities to see rugby is crucial to whetting their appetites for the World Cup they will host in five years.

"It's great to come over here and see what America has to offer," Taylor said. "They love their sports and they got right behind rugby.

"America has obviously got some great sports and they're fanatical about every sport they're involved in. It would be great to see US Rugby keep building.

"Leading into 2031, it's in a strong place to lay the foundation for what will be an awesome World Cup."

Kolisi also was positive about the future for rugby in the country and he hopes NFL teams might adopt the game as an offseason option, investing in existing American clubs.

"I really think Americans would love rugby if they get to see more of it and if it's shown a whole lot more on TV," Kolisi said. But I think it needs a lot of hard work obviously.

"I really believe if the NFL teams buy into rugby and if they become part-owners in the rugby clubs and if some of their players who don't get to play often, if they let them play rugby I think that would help the game a lot.

"Also I think it's a game that Americans would actually enjoy. They love physical sports. So I really think the more teams get to come and play here, the more people are invested in the rugby teams."

Kolisi hails Rassie: He reminds us where we come from

The fourth Test between South Africa and New Zealand marked Rassie Erasmus' 100th Test in charge of the Springoks and Kolisi hailed him as the reason why their side are as dominant as they are.

"We've got coach Rassie (Erasmus)," he said. "He knows us and gets us up. When he speaks to us he reminds us where we come from.

"The players who are in the group but not playing today, we do it for them, the guys who are injured and also for the people of South Africa who would love to have the opportunities we have."

articles.title: Henry Pollock: Northampton Saints star open to exploring opportunities in future and says Eddie Hearn's £1m valuation 'isn't a pressure'
articles.summary: Henry Pollock's contract with Northampton expires in summer 2027; Pollock's agent Eddie Hearn says the England forward merits a salary of more than £1m per year; Pollock says he is open to exploring all options
articles.body:
Pollock's focus remains on rugby and he is at the advanced stage of negotiations for a new contract with Gallagher Prem champions Northampton.

However, the 21-year-old is also looking to eventually broaden his horizons having signed for Eddie Hearn's Matchroom Talent Agency.

"I definitely want to go and live in different countries, explore new sports, explore new avenues," Pollock said.

"Eddie and the Matchroom team are constantly messaging me, calling me about different avenues and they've been great with that kind of stuff. I'm not going to say no to any opportunity.

"At the minute rugby is my main priority so I'm focusing on that in the near future, but as I said, you never know what's happening around the corner."

Hearn told Northampton in August that Pollock is "certainly a seven-figure player" because of the commercial clout he brings and the Lions flanker has taken the £1m-plus valuation in his stride.

"I don't see it as pressure," he said. "I see it as him doing his job. He's the best sports promoter in the world. The reason he's the best is because he gets his client what he deserves.

"Eddie's been great for me and he's given me so many avenues to get into. The way that he can give me access to loads of different stuff has been amazing.

"I have no bad words about him. The sport of rugby needs to change and hopefully this is a change."

While Pollock's options for his future remain vast, it is understood that he is close to remaining at Northampton.

While Pollock wants to remain at a club that has been "special" to him, he understands that, during his career, he may need to make "selfish" decisions for his trajectory.

"Northampton's been so great to me, I've been here my whole career and they've made me who I am. For me to stay here would be so special," said Pollock.

"Obviously, I know it's not as easy as that and I know there's lots of moving parts that come into play. I'm very open to new opportunities and I'm very open to exploring that.

"I'm so young so I think it's only right that I assess those options and find the best decision for myself.

"Your career is so short that you look back on yourself and you almost regret not exploring new avenues, exploring different things," he later added.

"I think for me, you almost have to be quite selfish in that aspect, think what's right for you. If that is staying here, then that's great, I'll be here for however long. If it's not, then I'll be open to new opportunities."

articles.title: Women's Super League: York Valkyrie win 12-0 at Leeds Rhinos to book Grand Final place vs defending champions Wigan Warriors
articles.summary: Tries from Liv Wood, Adaoha Akwiwu, in addition to penalty and conversion from Tara Jane Stanley sees York Valkyrie win Women's Super League semi-final at Leeds Rhinos; Watch Grand Final between Wigan and York live on Sky Sports on Sunday September 27 (5.30pm kick-off)
articles.body:
York will now face defending champions Wigan in the Grand Final at the Brick Community Stadium on Sunday September 27 (5.30pm kick-off), live on Sky Sports.

York, who were beaten 38-16 by Leeds on August 8, and 44-0 by Wigan a week later on August 15, have totally turned fortunes around since, defeating Leeds at home, St Helens away and Wigan at home before sealing semi-final success.

The opening 21 minutes proved scoreless at Headingley in a tight contest, before York's Liv Wood twisted, turned and wrestled over to ground the ball for a try in the 22nd minute. Tara Jane Stanley converted for the full haul.

As the first half drew to a close and with Leeds camped on the York try-line on the verge of a try, a grubber-kick on the last by Leeds' Ruby Walker proved a poor one and allowed Stanley to gather and run clear.

Instead, York were next to add points as Stanley struck a penalty superbly from distance for a lead of 8-0 three minutes from the end of the half.

Eight minutes into the second half, Stanley accelerated forward and forced her way over for York's second try and clear daylight on the scoreboard - but the Video Ref then proved via replays she lost control in the act of scoring to rule it out.

Buoyed by their reprieve, Leeds came back attacking hard at York, but Valkyrie defended superbly to keep their two-score lead intact.

On the hour mark, Leeds' Georgia Elliston powered her way over under the sticks for a try, but again the score was ruled out by the Video Ref, who ruled obstruction.

York then wrapped up victory through Adaoha Akwiwu's try as she burst through off a Stanley short-ball pass for a 12-0 advantage.

With six minutes remaining, Leeds' Ebony Stead appeared to charge over for a try out wide to give Rhinos brief hope, but for a third time on the night the Video Ref ruled out a score, as replays proved Stead had lost control of the ball while going over.

The contest ended on a sour note for York too, with the news Stanley - their standout performer on the night - had failed a Head Injury Assessment (HIA), ruling her out of the Grand Final.

Pryce: Nobody gave us a chance - we've made it against all odds

York Valkyrie head coach Leon Pryce to Sky Sports:

"This is unbelievable. Nobody gave us a chance.

"Everyone had written us off, and last week they were saying it was going to be another Saints vs Leeds game after Saints won here.

"We read the comments and used that as fuel. I don't think we got the respect we deserved, but they've been unbelievable.

"To come to Leeds in a semi-final against a really good squad and keep them to zero just shows.

"It was going to be about grit, toughness and determination.

"Against all odds we've got there and I couldn't be more proud.

"I've been proud of them all season, but the last four or five weeks we've really turned a corner and we don't want the season to end."

Wigan trio make up shortlist for 2026 Woman of Steel

Wigan Warriors will dominate the 2026 Woman of Steel awards, with three players from the reigning Women's Super League champions shortlisted for the competition's most prestigious individual honour.

Jenna Foubister , Eva Hunter and Megan Williams have all been named on the three-player shortlist ahead of Rugby League Awards Night in Manchester, which will take place on the evening of Tuesday September 29.

Foubister's nomination comes after another influential season at the heart of Wigan's attack in 2026. The 19-year-old half-back contributed a return of nine tries in 18 appearances across all competitions and has continued to establish herself as one of the leading playmakers in the women's game. Foubister also produced a Player of the Match performance in the Women's Challenge Cup Final at Wembley Stadium, creating two tries and providing three line-break assists as the Warriors lifted the trophy for a second time.

Reigning Woman of Steel Hunter has enjoyed another prolific campaign under Denis Betts, crossing for 23 tries in all competitions. The dynamic second-rower has continued to showcase her devastating pace, powerful ball-carrying and defensive intensity throughout the season, while also writing her name into the history books by becoming the first woman to score four tries in a Challenge Cup Final at Wembley Stadium.

Williams' place on the Woman of Steel shortlist follows a remarkable first two seasons with the Cherry & White, having quickly established herself as one of the competition's most consistent forwards. Since joining the club ahead of the 2025 campaign from St Helens, the England Knights international has become a key figure in Betts' side. The loose forward has scored four tries since the competition split into the Super Four phase, helping Wigan maintain their push for another historic season.

Watch the Women's Super League Grand Final between Wigan Warriors and York Valkyrie live on Sky Sports on Sunday September 27, with kick-off at 5.30pm.

articles.title: Super League play-off eliminator: Wakefield Trinity v Leigh Leopards kicks off 2026 play-offs
articles.summary: From unfancied to challenging at the top - Wakefield and Leigh meet in a Super League play-off on Friday, aiming to continue their respective trajectories.
articles.body:
Not so long ago, this was a fixture between two of Super League's unfancied teams.

Whether it was Wakefield battling at the bottom of the table, or Leigh fighting to even remain in Super League, these two sides rarely basked in optimism or bigger-picture successes on the field.

That has changed in recent times, however.

Trinity host Leigh in the first of this season's Super League play-off fixtures as they kick off the eliminator phase of the competition on Friday.

Neither have reached a Super League Grand Final - will 2026 be the year?

Wakefield win at Leigh to confirm home play-off

For Daryl Powell, his Wakefield side have done much to turn around their fortunes during his tenure.

His arrival at the club, which coincided with investment from owner Matt Ellis, started the upturn as Trinity won the Championship League Leaders' Shield in 2024 and returned to Super League for the 2025 season.

On their return to the top flight, the club offered no indication that they were happy to make up the numbers and they clinched a top-six place and a play-off spot at the first time of asking.

They fell short 12 months ago but with some smart recruitment, Wakefield have impressed this season. They battled with top spot for much of the campaign before eventually finishing fourth - their highest-ever Super League finish.

"I'm really proud of the whole organisation," Powell told BBC Radio Leeds.

"It comes from a lot of different people, from what we do with recruitment with Millsy [director of rugby Ste Mills] to the coaching team, which is like a band of brothers almost.

"The playing group have been outstanding."

Ultimately, Wakefield fell short of what would have been an outstanding League Leaders' Shield triumph, losing three of their final six games - including defeats by Leeds and Wigan.

As for where his side goes from here, Powell believes a spot in the Grand Final must be the aim.

"For me to be supporting all that and driving what we do as a culture, to give us a chance to be a top-four club, we want to be a consistent top-four club," he added.

"But then it's about getting [to the] play-offs, winning games in play-offs and having a crack at the Grand Final.

"I've really enjoyed my time here. It's an awesome club and I think it's going to be a special club for years to come."

Wakefield are not the only club with investment and momentum heading into the post-season and Friday's opponents have already broken into the upper echelons of Super League.

Since their return to the top flight in 2023, Leigh have rebranded as the Leopards and competed in the play-offs in each campaign since, in addition to winning the Challenge Cup.

Leopards boss Adrian Lam knows the tie is so important because of how close they have previously come to a spot in the Grand Final.

"[We have] finished fifth, fourth, third and then back to fifth again this season," he told BBC Radio Manchester.

"Two years in a row, people forget that we were 80 minutes away from Old Trafford and both at the hands of Wigan who ended up being in that Grand Final.

"Maybe if we had a different path then things might have been different, but we've always been striving to be better to find a different path and maybe get to Old Trafford."

Despite kicking off their season with victory against Leeds, Leigh lost eight out of the following 16 games in all competitions, before winning nine of 12 games to close out the regular campaign.

They were, however, defeated at home by Wakefield last week - but Lam is unmoved about such a statistic.

"Maybe this is the year but I've been grateful of the group and everyone's worked really hard," he added.

"We weren't great last week but that's OK, it's 'where there's life, there's hope' so here we go."

From the verge of quitting to Dream Team glory

Leigh's Umyla Hanley has just been named in his second successive Super League Dream Team - no mean feat given he has played just 17 games this season - and looks set to be part of England boss Brian McDermott's plans before the Rugby League World Cup, which starts in October.

Yet the 24-year-old's successes in the Leigh shirt, particularly since moving to centre, may never have happened at all and he may have been destined for a job as a builder having seen his opportunities with Wigan fizzle out.

"I grew up in Wigan, I'm from Wigan, came to the first team after the academy and just didn't really get that much game time and didn't really know how to handle it as a young lad," he told BBC Radio Manchester.

"I just kind of fell out of love with the game of rugby. I was going to hang it up and just work on site with my mates and have a laugh. But then Lammy gave me a call and he got me down to Leigh and the rest is history."

As for what inspired him not to quit rugby league, Hanley points to the camaraderie in the Leigh camp.

"It's when you're in the changing rooms with the lads after the game, before the game, even in training," he continued.

"Those kind of moments, you can't buy, and then when you perform well on the pitch as well it's just just a big bonus."

In only his second season in Super League, Wakefield's Caleb Hamlin-Uele has broken into the Dream Team ranks himself.

Even more impressive is that in that time he has made only 38 Super League appearances in total, but he bats away any suggestion that his excellent form is all his own doing.

"It's a testament to how hard I've worked and how hard everyone else behind me has worked, because it's not just me," he said.

"There's so many people that are behind closed doors that don't really get any limelight, but I'm grateful to have them all in my corner."

Hamlin-Uele, who missed last season's play-offs through injury, also missed last week's win at Leigh, but hopes he play his part on Friday.

"There's nothing more I want to do than just be with my brothers on that field, just trying to get us to Old Trafford," he said.

articles.title: Red Roses: Jess Breach, Alex Matthews return for England Women vs Canada as John Mitchell rings changes
articles.summary: John Mitchell's England Red Roses face Canada in first of three Tests on Saturday, playing side they beat at Twickenham to win 2025 Women's Rugby World Cup; Red Roses face Canada in WXV Global Series on Saturday in Exeter, and then away on Friday October 16 and Friday October 23
articles.body:
Breach and Matthews, both of whom played major roles in 2025's Women's Rugby World Cup glory - as England beat Canada in the final - come into the side on the right wing and at No 8 respectively.

Mitchell's side face Canada in Tests on Saturday in Exeter, Friday October 16 in Toronto, and Friday October 23 in Ottawa. They also face New Zealand on Saturday September 26 at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham.

Hooker Bryony Field scored on her international debut last weekend in the dominant win over Australia and earns a maiden start in an all-changed front row featuring Hannah Botterman and Maud Muir. Morwenna Talling is also back among the starting contingent from the second row.

Lucy Packer - another try scorer against the Wallaroos - is named at scrum-half with fly-half Zoe Harrison outside her. Helena Rowland is reinstated to the midfield alongside captain Meg Jones.

Three Exeter Chiefs players - Claudia Moloney-MacDonald, Maddie Feaunati and Flo Robinson - are in the squad as the Red Roses prepare to play at their club stadium, Sandy Park, for the first time since September 2023.

"This is the first Test of an exciting three-Test series between the No 1 and No 3 teams in the world," head coach Mitchell said.

"You need rivalries in our sport and our rivalry with Canada is one that has evolved to a great level. They are a well-coached team who will bring a different challenge to the one Australia presented. We will be expected to raise our standards."

England's squad contains 974 Test caps, while 14 players in the matchday 23 were involved in the World Cup final triumph over Canada at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham.

articles.title: Joe Marchant sets sights on England comeback after Sale arrival
articles.summary: Joe Marchant is determined to convince England head coach Steve Borthwick of his Test credentials and convert his famous father-in-law to Sale's cause.
articles.body:
"I've had a couple of near slip-ups, which I didn't tell any of the lads, where I'm just saying the things you'd say there," he says of training with his new Sale team-mates after three years at Paris-based Stade Francais.

"You can feel the words coming out wrong.

"For a high ball in France, you'd say 'j'ai', meaning 'I have'.

"So I have had to style that out and turn it into 'Joe's'."

Marchant's immersion in French life was swift and total.

He won the most recent of his 26 England caps in the third-place play-off win over Argentina at the 2023 Rugby World Cup. He had been head coach Steve Borthwick's first-choice outside centre throughout the tournament, starting every match bar the pool-stage thrashing of Chile.

But, as England took a lap of honour at Stade de France, Marchant was straight into Top 14 life and the Test exile that accompanies it.

"It was a bit of a strange one, everyone was going home and for me Paris was my new home," the 30-year-old remembers.

"We finished on the Saturday with the boys [England] and I had the team photo with Stade on the Tuesday, so it was just an on-to-the-next mentality."

Alongside the language, Marchant picked up plenty on the pitch during his stint in France. He feels he is a more assertive and communicative player than the one that left Harlequins. The Top 14 pushed him physically as well.

"It is such an intense league," he says. "Every weekend, there's someone who is at least 150kg who always sits out of a five man line-out, and you just have to get ready for that coming every week."

What's coming next in England is less predictable.

Borthwick has asked Marchant, like fellow Sale new boy Courtney Lawes, to prove himself in the Prem before any return to the Test fold.

"Steve and I have had a couple of chats here and there. Nothing crazy, but just a couple of chats," says Marchant.

"That was the main message. Get back on the field and play and see where we go.

"I want to play for England, that's what I want to do. I'm proud to have played for England and I don't want it to be my last time at that World Cup. I want to play again."

Marchant well knows how precious and precarious a Test career can be.

His decision to move to Stade Francais was partly motivated by a chat with Borthwick's predecessor Eddie Jones.

"There were those conversations just before the Autumn Internationals [in 2022] that I wasn't fitting the mould and I wasn't going to play in the World Cup," says Marchant.

"The Stade offer was a good offer that, on the back of the England stuff, seemed like the right thing to do.

"Then three weeks later, Eddie wasn't with England any more."

In the aftermath of Twickenham jeers and a Springbok defeat, Jones had been sacked. Marchant may have signed with Stade for the following season, but Borthwick was still a fan.

"Steve brought me in and we had a really honest chat about who I am as a player, my decision to go abroad and who I am as a person," says Marchant, of his 2023 return to the England fold.

"They were all really positive. From that, we just got pretty aligned. He knew what he wanted from me and how to get it. For me, I just felt like it was really good clarity on what I need to do to get into that England shirt."

Marchant, a rangy runner with an excellent nose for an angle or support line and an impressive aerial game, is an intriguing addition to England's existing midfield options.

Sale, with ambitions to play more expansively after significant squad investment, will hope to provide a platform for both Marchant and Lawes to make their cases a year out from the next Rugby World Cup.

They begin at home to Bristol on Saturday, 26 September. The match away to Newcastle Red Bulls also looms large in Marchant's domestic calendar.

His wife Hollie is the daughter of former Newcastle and England football striker Alan Shearer.

"Yeah, maybe," says Marchant about whether his father-in-law will be down at the Corpacq Stadium to watch him.

"I think the Newcastle game in October will probably be more likely. It's a bit closer to Newcastle.

"Hopefully he's supporting Sale. If he's not, that's not really 'play on'."

Converting Shearer, convincing Borthwick, continuing a Test career - there is plenty to play for for Marchant this season.
